title: Fort Dearborn, Building by Building
premise: The last full day of the first Fort Dearborn, 14 August 1812, from sunrise to sunset. See every building on Captain Whistler's 1808 drawing while the soldiers pack to leave. Twelve stops.

opening.text:
JAUNT: FORT DEARBORN, BUILDING BY BUILDING. It is Friday, 14 August 1812. This is the last full day of the first Fort Dearborn. The United States built this fort in 1803. Captain John Whistler and his soldiers marched here from Detroit. They built it out of logs on the south bank of the Chicago River. In 1808 Whistler drew a picture of every building. Since 1810 the fort's leader has been Captain Nathan Heald. He has more than sixty soldiers.

In June the United States went to war with Britain. Five days ago, a general sent an order: leave the fort. Tomorrow morning the soldiers will march out of the gate. Today everyone is packing up.

There are twelve stops, from sunrise to sunset. By tomorrow night, all but one of these buildings will be burned. Watch for the one that lasts.

stops.text: It is 14 August 1812, at sunrise. This is the first Fort Dearborn, seen from outside. Captain Whistler's soldiers came to this bend in the river in 1803. They built the whole fort out of logs with their own hands. A visitor in 1809 called it the neatest and best wooden fort in the country. There are soldiers' houses around a square. There are two tall gun towers at opposite corners. Two rows of log walls go all the way around. Now the order has come to leave. Tomorrow everyone inside will go. Today is their last full day here.

It is six in the morning, at the main gate on the south side. A girl who lived here remembered that the gates shut at sunset. Look at the two rows of log walls. If an enemy climbed over the first wall, he would be stuck in a narrow space. Soldiers in the towers could fire at him there. Whistler built this fort to hold off an attack. But nobody plans to stay and fight now. The order is to march out, and this is the gate they will use. Walk through the gate and step inside to where the soldiers live.

It is seven in the morning, just inside the gate. The soldiers' houses stand on both sides. They are two stories tall, with porches facing the open square. The first soldiers here built the fort themselves. When their time in the army ended, they all signed up again. This fort was very far from anywhere. Whistler wrote that he had sixty-six men but not enough clothes for all of them. He even said the only flute for the band had been lost. This morning the soldiers are packing for the long march to Fort Wayne.

It is half past eight, on the open square. In the middle stands a tall flagpole. On the east side is the house of the fort's leader, Captain Nathan Heald. In 1811 he brought his new wife, Rebekah, to live here. A book says she and Mrs. Helm played a game like badminton here last spring. In May, the Healds' baby boy was born but did not live. The order to leave came on 9 August. It was read out loud the next morning, right here. The officers asked Heald to stay and make the fort stronger. But Heald chose to obey the order.

It is ten o'clock, at the officers' house, across from the leader's house. Three men live here. Lieutenant Linai Helm is second in charge. His wife, Margaret, is the stepdaughter of John Kinzie, the trader across the river. Ensign George Ronan is the youngest officer. He came straight from army school. Dr. Isaac Van Voorhis is the fort's young doctor, only twenty-two. Last fall he wrote that one day millions of people would live here. He was right. Sadly, Ronan and the doctor will not live through tomorrow, and Helm will be taken prisoner.

It is eleven o'clock, on the north side. Ahead is the magazine, where the gunpowder is kept. It is a small building made of brick, in a fort made of logs. Next to it is a gun tower and a small side gate. When the fort burns, this little brick building will be the only one left standing. But the fort's extra gunpowder is not here anymore. Last night it was carried out in secret to the north-east corner. Then it was dropped down a well.

It is noon, at the north-east corner. From here a covered path once ran down to the river. It let soldiers get water safely during an attack. A well was dug inside it. Last night the soldiers threw the extra gunpowder and broken guns down the well. They poured the whiskey into the river. Captain Heald did not want anyone to use those things against them. It was no secret. By morning, people said, the river water tasted like whiskey. Now everyone outside the fort knows the extra guns are gone.

It is half past one, outside the log walls on the south-east side. Here stood a store, a garden, and a shop where the soldiers' guns were fixed. One trader was allowed to sell things to the soldiers. Since January, that was John Kinzie and his partner. Behind you rises the south-east gun tower. Whistler's drawing put the towers on two opposite corners. A book written forty years later remembered them both on the south side. People do not always remember things the same way. South of here, the gardens are full of food nobody will stay to eat.

It is three in the afternoon, in the leader's gardens, south of the fort. In the early years, people grew melons, fruit and vegetables here. Whistler had all the bushes cleared for a long way around the fort, so nobody could sneak up. Past the gardens is a big open field of grass and a line of trees by the river. Tomorrow the soldiers and families will go the other way. They will walk east to the lake, then south along the beach.

It is half past four, west of the fort, among the government buildings. There is a trading house, a few homes, a bakery and the stables. The trading house is the government's own store. Today Captain Heald gave away all the goods in the store. His report says he "delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store". He also gave away food the soldiers could not carry. Blankets, cloth and paints went out the door. In April, the townspeople made one log house stronger. They boarded up its porches and cut holes to look out, and guards watched at night. Now the store shelves are empty.

It is six in the evening, at the dock below the river bank. Here boats tied up and the fort's supplies were unloaded. In 1808 Whistler said the fort was safe from a surprise attack. He said only one thing was in the way: the houses across the river. The biggest of those houses belongs to John Kinzie. His family will not march with the soldiers tomorrow. They will leave by boat. Walk along the bank and look at the house as the sun goes down on the fort's last night.

It is sunset. Across the river is John Kinzie's house, with three more houses to the west. Kinzie sells to the soldiers and lives close enough to shout to the gate. Behind you, the gates are shutting at sunset, for the last time. Tomorrow at nine in the morning they will open. The band will play slow, sad music, and the soldiers will walk out. The next day the fort will be set on fire. Only the brick magazine will last. The army will come back in 1816 and build a new fort here.

legs.story: Walk around the west side to the main gate on the south.

legs.note: Through both gates, into the fort.

legs.story: Walk across the open square to the east side.
Turn around. The west side faces the leader's door.
Go to the north side of the square.

legs.note: Up over the pickets to the north-east corner, above the river.
Outside the pickets, round to the south-east.

legs.story: Go north to the river bank.
Walk along the bank to face the Kinzie house.

endings.text: On 15 August 1812 the soldiers and families marched out of the gate. Captain Heald wrote later that the warriors set fire to the fort and left, taking prisoners with them. Seven months later, a visitor found the brick magazine still standing. Everything else Whistler built had burned down. For four years the place was quiet and empty. Then the army came back in 1816 and built a new fort on the same ground. To follow the soldiers out of the gate on the morning of the 15th, take the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

keepsake.title: Whistler's draught of Fort Dearborn, 1808
keepsake.text: 'At this time the Garrison (except the Houses on the Opisite side of the river being somewhat in the way) is perfectly secure from any ambuscade or Barrier.' Captain John Whistler, 20 February 1808.

evidence.text: Quaife (1913), from Swearingen's journal: 'The troops reached the Chicago River at two o'clock on the afternoon of August 17, after a march of twenty-four miles from their last camping-place on the Little Calumet.' 'The river bank was eight feet high at the point where the fort was to be built, a half-mile above the mouth of the stream.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. V, the founding of the fort (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraph beginning 'The troops reached the Chicago River')

evidence.text: William Johnston, who came from Fort Wayne in the spring of 1809, as Quaife (1913) quotes him: Fort Dearborn was 'the neatest and best wooden garrison in the United States,' a fact which did 'great honor to Capt. John Whistler who planned and built it.' Whistler still had the men he built it with: 'Although their term of enlistment had expired they had all re-enlisted'.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the paragraph on Whistler's removal and Johnston's visit (Gutenberg #69274 plain text)

evidence.text: Quaife (1913), from Cooper and Whistler's draught: 'The barracks and other structures for the accommodation of the garrison were built around the four sides of a quadrangle, facing inward toward the center. Two blockhouses, one containing two small cannon, the other containing one, stood at the northwestern and southeastern corners of the quadrangle, and the whole was inclosed within a double row of palisades'. 'Thus if an enemy should scale the first row he would only find himself within a narrow inclosure between that and the second which was swept at every point by the fire from the blockhouses.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure')

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): the barracks 'were two stories in height, with shingled roofs and covered galleries, and occupied the middle of each side of the inclosure facing toward the parade ground, in the center of which stood a lofty flagstaff. The commanding officer's quarters stood on the east side, and directly opposite were those for the subordinate officers. The main gateway of the stockade was at the middle of the south side and was flanked on either side by the main barracks for the common soldiers.' Whistler's own note: 'the Barracks are two storeys high with shingled Roofs and Galliaries fronting the parade.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text)

evidence.text: Whistler's letters to Colonel Kingsbury, as Quaife (1913) gives them: the whip-saw 'can be of little use without files, for oak is the only saw timber available at Chicago.' 'Fifty-six suits of clothing have been received, but he has sixty-six men to supply. He has two fifers but the only fife has been lost. Watch coats are needed very badly.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the paragraph beginning 'Two weeks after Kingsbury's letter'

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): Heald married 'Rebekah Wells, the daughter of Colonel Samuel Wells and the niece of Captain William Wells' on 23 May 1811, and 'in June the commander reached Chicago with his bride'. Heald's journal: 'On the 4th of May, 1812, we had a son born dead for the want of a skilful Midwife.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VII, the paragraphs on Heald's marriage and his journal (Gutenberg #69274 plain text); Appendix III, Heald's journal

evidence.text: Wau-Bun (1856): in the spring of 1812 two visitors to the commanding officer, 'As they passed through the quarters, they saw Mrs. Heald and Mrs. Helm playing at battledoor.' One of them, Nau-non-gee, said to the interpreter: 'The white chiefs' wives are amusing themselves very much; it will not be long before they are hoeing in our corn-fields!' 'This was considered at the time an idle threat'. 'Some months after, how bitterly was it remembered!'
evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'After the 15th of August'

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): Ensign George Ronan was 'a young cadet direct from West Point', ordered to Fort Dearborn in March 1811; Lieutenant Linai T. Helm came from Detroit at his own request, for 'his straitened financial circumstances and the cheaper cost of living at Fort Dearborn as compared with Detroit.' Surgeon's mate Isaac Van Voorhis, writing in October 1811: 'In my solitary walks I contemplate what a great and powerful republic will yet arise in this new world. Here, I say, will be the seat of millions yet unborn'. Quaife: 'The man who at the age of twenty-two could pen these lines'. Heald's report: 'Ensign George Ronan and Doctor Isaac V. Van Voorhis of my company, with Captain Wells of Fort Wayne' were killed; Helm was taken prisoner.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VII, the paragraph beginning 'In March, 1811'; ch. X, the paragraph on Van Voorhis; Appendix IV, Heald's report

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'The building opposite was in part devoted to barracks for the soldiers and in part to housing the contractor's store of supplies. Between this building and the northwestern blockhouse stood the magazine, a small structure made of brick. This alone defied the fire which destroyed the fort at the time of the massacre.' 'A small wicket gate in the stockade gave ingress and egress near the northwestern blockhouse.' Robert Dickson, through Chicago in March 1813, found 'two brass cannon, one dismounted, the other on wheels but in the river. The powder magazine was in a good state of preservation'.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); ch. IX, the paragraph on Dickson's visit

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'From the northeast corner of the stockade a covered way led to the river, securing thus to the garrison access in safety to the water in time of attack.' Whistler's index lists 'Covered Way to procure Water' and 'Gutters to carry off the Water' as 'Omited in their places'. Wau-Bun remembers 'a sally-port, or subterranean passage from the parade-ground to the river', and on 13 August 1812 'the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency'.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Whistler's draught (1808) and Quaife (1913) put the two blockhouses at the north-west and south-east corners. Wau-Bun (1856), written over forty years after the fort burned, remembers it otherwise: 'It had two block-houses on the southern side, and on the northern a sally-port'.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the paragraph beginning 'The fort was differently constructed'

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'Whistler's drawing represents a considerable number of houses and outbuildings ranged around the fort devoted to various purposes. Among these are houses for the interpreter and for the factor's department, an armorer's shop, a merchant's shop, and a bake shop, besides several stables on the south side'. Whistler's index numbers them: 'Agents House', 'Factors House', 'Interpreters House', 'Armerers Shop', 'Merchants Shop', 'Bake House', 'Stables'.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text)

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'To the south of the fort were the commanding officer's gardens in which, in Cooper's time, melons and other small fruit and vegetables were raised.' Whistler, 1808: on the north and west 'there has been a quantity of underwood and shruby Bushes such as prickly Ash &c. they are now cut down and cleared off, all within one Fourth of a Mile of the Garrison.' To the south and south-west 'is a large parraria'.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text), Whistler's note

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'A short distance to the southwest were two log houses, one occupied by Matthew Irwin, the United States factor, and the other by Charles Jouett, the Indian agent.' Wau-Bun (1856) on the Agency House in April 1812: 'It was an old-fashioned log building, with a hall running through the centre, and one large room on each side. Piazzas extended the whole length of the building in front and rear. These were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the paragraph beginning 'It was an old-fashioned log building'

evidence.text: Whistler, 20 February 1808, closing his note to the draught: 'At this time the Garrison (except the Houses on the Opisite side of the river being somewhat in the way) is perfectly secure from any ambuscade or Barrier.' His index numbers the 'Wharf of said River' and 'John Kinzie Esq. House on the opisite side River'. He had already had a picket fence across the river taken up, since it 'might serve as a Barrier against the Garrison', and 'replaced with a common rail fence.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text), Whistler's note

evidence.text: Heald's report, 23 October 1812: 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' Quaife (1913): 'over Chicago silence and desolation reigned supreme.' The second fort went up on the same ground in 1816.
evidence.locator: Quaife, Appendix IV, Heald's report; ch. IX, the paragraph beginning 'several villages'

evidence.text: Heald's journal: 'On the 9th of Augt, 1812, rec'd orders from Genl Wm. Hull to evacuate the Post of Chicago and proceed with my Command to Detroit.' Quaife: 'The next day the Indian runner. Winnemac, delivered to Captain Heald at Fort Dearborn his order for the evacuation.' Wau-Bun puts the runner, Winnemeg or Catfish, a Potawatomi, at the post on the 7th, bringing despatches that 'announced the declaration of war between the United States and Great Britain'. Wau-Bun: 'The order for evacuating the post was read next morning upon parade', and the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Quaife defends Heald: 'Obedience to orders is the primary duty of a soldier.'
evidence.locator: Quaife Appendix III (Heald's journal) and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 14th, I delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Wau-Bun, which dates it the 13th: 'the goods, consisting of blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints, etc., were distributed, as stipulated.'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The surplus arms and ammunition I thought proper to destroy, fearing they would make bad use of it if put in their possession. I also destroyed all the liquor on hand after they began to collect.' Wau-Bun: 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency; the remainder was transported as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The noise betrayed it, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march: a part of the Miamies were detached in front, and the remainder in our rear, as guards, under the direction of Captain Wells. The situation of the country rendered it necessary for us to take the beach, with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right, at about 100 yards distance.' Wau-Bun: 'As the troops left the fort, the band struck up the Dead March', and Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' Mrs. Kinzie's boat 'had scarcely reached the mouth of the river, which, it will be recollected, was here half a mile below the fort, when another messenger from To-pee-nee-bee arrived to detain them where they were.' Quaife lists the order: Wells and part of the Miamis, the garrison, the women and children, the twelve Chicago militia.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'At half-past five o'clock on the morning of July 14, 1803, the troops set out from Detroit'; they 'reached the Chicago River at two o'clock on the afternoon of August 17'. The fort: 'The barracks and other structures for the accommodation of the garrison were built around the four sides of a quadrangle', with 'Two blockhouses' and 'a double row of palisades'. In April 1810 Captain John Whistler was moved to Detroit, and 'Captain Nathan Heald, who, in turn, succeeded Whistler at Fort Dearborn'. Heald's report: 'Our strength was fifty-four regulars and twelve militia'.
evidence.locator: Quaife 1913, the chapters on the building of the fort, the garrison of 1810 and the evacuation, Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun (1856): 'On the north side of the main stream, but quite near its junction with Lake Michigan, stood (as has already been described) the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie.' 'The fort was situated on the southern bank, directly opposite this mansion'. The Chicago Reader (2018): in January 1812 Heald made 'Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth' the exclusive fort sutlers. Kirkland (1893): Margaret Helm was the 'step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.
evidence.locator: Wau-Bun, the April section; the Reader, the sutler paragraph; Kirkland, the Helm narrative

evidence.text: Victoire Porthier, a girl inside the fort, as Andreas printed her and Kirkland reprints: 'My sister Madeline and I saw the fight between John Kinzie and Lalime, when Lalime was killed. It was sunset, when they used to shut the gates of the fort. Kinzie and Lalime came out together, and soon we heard Lieutenant Helm call out for Mr. Kinzie to look out for Lalime, as he had a pistol. Quick we saw the men come together. We heard the pistol go off and saw the smoke. Then they fell down together. I don't know as Lalime got up at all, but Kinzie got home pretty quick. Blood was running from his shoulder, where Lalime had shot him. In the night he packed up some things and my father took him to Milwaukee'. 'I don't know what the quarrel was about. It was an old one--business, I guess.'
evidence.locator: Appendix F, 'The Bones of John Lalime', Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 6120-6540, Mrs. Porthier's statement

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'Meanwhile war had been declared by Congress on June 18'. 'News of the declaration of war was received at Fort Dearborn toward the middle of July.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, the chapter on the evacuation (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraphs on Hull's march and on the news reaching Fort Dearborn)

evidence.text: The tour is set on 14 August 1812, the last full day before the march of the 15th, and walks the fort from daybreak to sunset. Heald's report puts the giving-out of the factory goods on the 14th; Wau-Bun puts the destruction of the ammunition and liquor on the evening before. The hours of the stops are the jaunt's pacing; no source gives them.
evidence.reasoning: The date is the eve of the march Heald dates 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning'; the hours are chosen to walk the day in order, not recorded.
